article_text:
A “ Dirty Dancing ” sequel with Jennifer Grey might sound like another shiny legacy sequel to a Hollywood classic, but producer Nina Jacobson is working to develop a follow-up that honors the grit and raw feeling of the 1987 original.

“I remember when I first saw it, it seemed like very glossy entertainment. Now it feels like kind of an indie. They take a lot of risks and they touch a lot of topics that people don’t touch in movies anymore,” Jacobson said during a panel at IndieWire ‘s Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit presented by AT&T. “If you tried to just slip by an abortion subplot in a romantic movie now, I think you’d get a lot of notes on that.”

Jacobson took part in a conversation with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang at the event on Saturday in Los Angeles. Her film production company Color Force , where she is a producer and partner, is also behind FX’s “Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. & Carolyn Bessette” and Lionsgate’s upcoming “Hunger Games” prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Earlier this year, Color Force also came aboard as producers for Lionsgate’s “Dirty Dancing” follow-up (though not “Dirty Dancing 2,” lest one forget “Havana Nights”), which will see Grey return as Frances “Baby” Houseman for a new ‘90s-set romance featuring another young cast.

“Grey has incredible insights into why she thinks [‘Dirty Dancing’] has lasted so much or what it is about her character that spoke so much to people and still does,” Jacobson said. “We were talking about this with adaptations: a movie can’t be just like the book, or a show can’t be just like the book that you are adapting. But it should make you feel the way the book did, and it should feel the way the book felt. [We are] trying to chase the feeling of that original movie. … Being able to tell a young love story that could take some of those risks but also inspire those feelings felt like an incredible chance for us.”

Along with Grey’s lead turn, “Dirty Dancing” is also defined by a co-lead turn by Patrick Swayze, as the concentrated dancer Johnny Castle that teaches Baby how to have the time of her life. Swayze died in 2009 of pancreatic cancer and Jacobson is intent on honoring the late star’s legacy with the sequel.

“That’s one of the things that you really have to focus on: how to let people mourn him in a movie,” Jacobson said. Then she added an assurance: “And don’t worry, we won’t be bringing him back with AI .”

Along with “Dirty Dancing,” Jacobson also shared details about the newly announced “Crazy Rich Asians” HBO series, which will draw from Kevin Kwan’s book series to further continue the story seen in the hit 2018 romantic comedy adaptation. While a second film was long speculated about, the producer explained why an ongoing TV series was the approach that was taken for the property’s return.

“We’ve struggled with trying to adapt it as a feature. It’s actually very hard to do a sequel to a romantic comedy because you resolve the central emotional conflict,” she said. “And, honestly, part of it was that none of the folks from the feature side who were there when we made the original were still there. … They didn’t necessarily have that appetite, whereas there was an enormous appetite over at HBO for the books. There’s so much in the books that you have to subtract because the books have this great big cast of characters and all these crazy melodramatic twists and turns. It’s very well-suited to television.”

“It was unimaginable if we tried to do this right after the movie came out: the idea that you could get all of these people who all blew up afterwards to do a TV show together,” Jacobson continued. “But now everybody misses everybody else. Television really is one of the best ways for us to do a reunion because it’s very hard to address all the things people liked about the movie in a sequel.”

Along with the conversation with Jacobson, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit also included a keynote by directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, diving into the production of their sci-fi blockbuster “Project Hail Mary,” and a one-on-one with Bill Hader on what he learned making his upcoming feature debut “They Know.”

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. article_text:
Archives – October 21, 2025

Christian Caujolle has died yesterday. He was the best of us.

Of the generation that discovered and began writing about photography in the 1970s, he was the most brilliant, the most cultured, the most passionate, and the most daring, simultaneously favoring social photography and fine art photography.

A very close friendship had long bound us together, it was not always easy between the man behind the images of Libération and Vu and the editor of PHOTO . Yet, I have lost count of those endless lunches where we exchanged all our ideas, anecdotes, and comments.

In our archives, you will discover the hundred or so texts he wrote for L’Oeil de la Photographie .

He had been in bad shape for a long time. Lately, it has been even worse, and his emails and calls were desperate.

We will come back to him.

Love to you, Christian!

Jean-Jacques Naudet

article_text:
MTA Arts & Design, the art-focused organization that facilitates the creation of artworks for New York’s mass transit system, has revealed the latest three artists to receive commissions: Ivan Forde , Trevor Paglen , and Howardena Pindell .

Forde will create a large-scale mosaic installation for the Broadway Junction subway station. A release describes the artwork, titled Bedtime Story for Brownsville: The Fish Who Carried the Moon (2026), as “a mythic bedtime story in which flying fish carry the Moon from the ocean floor to the sky.” It will be partially set in the entrance to the L train and a pedestrian bridge that extends above Van Sinderen Avenue. Forde said he hopes the work “brings joy, bravery, and pride to young families in Brownsville and its sister neighborhoods, intergenerational community members, local and international travelers alike.”

Paglen’s commission will appear in a pedestrian overpass and a new parking garage at the Southeast stop of the Metro-North train system. Titled Perennial (2026), it will see the artist photograph flora near the station, then run those images through an algorithm that will analyze the flowers’ colors. The end result will look like an abstracted spectrum. Paglen said the work is meant to “reflect on the increasingly blurred boundaries between human and machine perception.”

Pindell’s commission also has its roots in pictures of flowers and is being produced for the Metro-North’s Botanical Garden station. Her glass installation is based on photos she took at the New York Botanical Garden last summer; she then edited the pictures and ported the results over to glass. The results occasionally veer into abstraction. Pindell said the work “adds a little joy ahead of getting to the garden, especially if you investigate where each of the images come from—such as the flowers, the squirrels, or the greenhouse.”

“These artists are among the most compelling voices in contemporary art today,” said Tina Vaz, director of MTA Arts & Design, said in a statement. “By bringing their work into the public realm, we affirm our commitment to making museum-quality art part of New Yorkers’ daily lives and to transforming transit spaces into environments of beauty, imagination, and cultural resonance.”

Tratta dall’omonima rassegna ideata dall’artista e curatore indipendente Francesco Arena , la rubrica OTHER IDENTITY – Altre forme di identità culturali e pubbliche vuole essere una cartina al tornasole capace di misurare lo stato di una nuova e più attuale grammatica visiva, presentando il lavoro di autori e artisti che operano con i linguaggi della fotografia, del video e della performance, per indagare i temi dell’identità e dell’autorappresentazione. Questa settimana intervistiamo Eric Pickersgill .

Other Identity: Eric Pickersgill

Il nostro privato è pubblico e la rappresentazione di noi stessi si modifica e si spettacolarizza continuamente in ogni nostro agire. Qual è la tua rappresentazione di arte?

«La mia rappresentazione dell’arte è quella di uno specchio critico che rivela la natura performativa dell’esistenza contemporanea. L’arte, per me, funziona sia come documento sia come intervento: cattura i modi in cui, inconsciamente, mettiamo in scena le nostre identità e, al tempo stesso, interrompe queste performance per generare consapevolezza.

Nel mio lavoro, in particolare REMOVED , mi interessa come l’atto stesso di fare arte diventi una performance che smaschera altre performance. Quando rimuovo fisicamente i dispositivi dalle mani delle persone prima di fotografarle, creo un momento di rivelazione in cui emerge la dimensione teatrale delle nostre interazioni quotidiane. Le immagini che ne derivano mostrano corpi che continuano a trattenere dispositivi fantasma, rivelando quanto profondamente la tecnologia abbia coreografato i nostri gesti e la nostra presenza sociale.

L’arte diventa così un mezzo per rendere visibili i copioni invisibili che seguiamo: i comportamenti appresi, le pose inconsce, il modo in cui ci disponiamo quando pensiamo di essere osservati o registrati. Non si tratta solo di documentare questi fenomeni, ma di creare esperienze che permettano agli spettatori di riconoscere questi schemi nelle proprie vite».

Creiamo delle vere e proprie identità di genere che ognuno di noi sceglie in corrispondenza delle caratteristiche che vuole evidenziare, così forniamo tracce. Qual è la tua “identità” nell’arte contemporanea?

«La mia identità nell’arte contemporanea è quella di un archeologo del comportamento e di un interventista sociale. Scavo nei modi sottili in cui la tecnologia rimodella l’interazione umana e presento queste scoperte attraverso interruzioni attentamente orchestrate della normalità.

Mi posiziono come qualcuno che rende lo familiare estraneo. La mia pratica consiste nell’inserirmi in scenari quotidiani—cene di famiglia, spazi pubblici, momenti intimi—e nel creare piccole fratture che rivelano verità più ampie su come mettiamo in scena noi stessi nell’era digitale. Che si tratti di rimuovere fisicamente i dispositivi dalle mani o di rifiutarmi di partecipare a foto di famiglia in posa, utilizzo la mia presenza sia come catalizzatore sia come critica.

Questa identità affonda le sue radici nella curiosità più che nel giudizio. Non sto condannando l’uso della tecnologia, ma indagando su come essa ci trasformi. Il mio lavoro traccia in tempo reale l’evoluzione del gesto umano, dell’attenzione e della presenza, creando una sorta di archivio antropologico di questo momento senza precedenti nella storia, in cui i dispositivi sono diventati estensioni dei nostri corpi.

Mi vedo come un traduttore: trasformo preoccupazioni astratte sulla cultura digitale in esperienze viscerali e visive che gli spettatori possono percepire nei propri corpi».

Quanto conta per te l’importanza dell’apparenza sociale e pubblica?

«L’apparenza sociale e pubblica è centrale nel mio lavoro, anche se non nel senso convenzionale dell’autopromozione. Ciò che mi affascina è piuttosto il divario tra come appariamo e come realmente esistiamo—lo spazio tra l’identità performata e l’esperienza vissuta.

La mia pratica gioca deliberatamente con visibilità e invisibilità. In REMOVED rendo visibile il controllo invisibile che i nostri dispositivi esercitano su di noi. Nella serie INTERVENTION , mi rendo volutamente assente dalle foto di famiglia, creando una consapevolezza scomoda su come mettiamo in scena la nostra felicità per la documentazione.

“L’importanza” non sta nel costruire un’immagine pubblica perfetta, ma nel comprendere come l’apparenza pubblica funzioni come una forma d’arte contemporanea. Ogni post sui social, ogni foto di famiglia, ogni momento in cui teniamo in mano il telefono diventa una sorta di performance artistica. Il mio compito, come artista, è analizzare queste performance, inclusa la mia.

Sono interessato al paradosso dell’autenticità: più cerchiamo di apparire autentici online, più diventiamo performativi. La mia presenza pubblica come artista consiste nell’essere trasparente riguardo a questa contraddizione, piuttosto che cercare di risolverla».

Il richiamo, il plagio, la riedizione, il ready made dell’iconografia di un’identità legata al passato, al presente e al contemporaneo sono messi costantemente in discussione in una ricerca affannosa di una nuova identificazione del sé, di un nuovo valore di rappresentazione. Qual è il tuo valore di rappresentazione oggi?

«Mi rappresento come un artista che genera un disagio produttivo. Il mio valore risiede nel creare momenti di riconoscimento che spostano il modo in cui le persone percepiscono i propri comportamenti e le proprie relazioni.

Più che fornire risposte, creo esperienze che stimolano domande. Quando gli spettatori osservano le mie fotografie di persone che tengono in mano telefoni invisibili, spesso reagiscono controllando istintivamente i propri dispositivi. È proprio in quella risposta involontaria che avviene il vero lavoro—nel momento del riconoscimento di sé.

Mi rappresento al tempo stesso come insider e outsider rispetto ai fenomeni che documento. Non sono esente dalla dipendenza dagli schermi o dalla compulsione a documentare la mia vita, ma utilizzo la mia posizione interna a questi sistemi per generare una distanza critica. Il mio valore rappresentativo sta nella capacità di essere contemporaneamente implicato e analitico nei confronti della cultura digitale.

Il mio lavoro si propone come una sorta di testimonianza documentaria—non di ciò che è stato, ma di ciò che sta accadendo ora, in questo momento straordinario di integrazione tecnologica. Mi rappresento come qualcuno che sta creando un archivio del presente per una futura comprensione».

ll nostro “agire” pubblico, anche con un’opera d’arte, travolge il nostro quotidiano, la nostra vita intima, i nostri sentimenti o, meglio, la riproduzione di tutto ciò che siamo e proviamo ad apparire nei confronti del mondo. Tu ti definisci un’artista agli occhi del mondo?

«Sì, ma con la consapevolezza che oggi la definizione di “artista” è diventata un’identità più complessa. Essere artista significa oggi essere al contempo creatore e contenuto, osservatore e osservato, critico e partecipante nei sistemi che si analizzano.

Il mondo si aspetta sempre più che gli artisti siano dei veri e propri brand, che mantengano una visibilità costante e che mettano in scena la propria identità sulle diverse piattaforme. Io affronto questa situazione facendo della mia pratica artistica stessa un’indagine su queste aspettative. Il mio lavoro mette in discussione i sistemi stessi che oggi definiscono il successo e la visibilità artistica.

Mi definisco un artista che opera nello spazio tra sé privato e persona pubblica, investigando come questi confini si siano dissolti nell’era digitale. La mia identità artistica è inseparabile dall’indagine sulle performance dell’identità stessa.

Gli “occhi del mondo” sono ormai mediati da schermi, algoritmi e raccolta dati. Essere artista agli occhi del mondo significa accettare che il proprio lavoro venga filtrato attraverso gli stessi sistemi tecnologici che esso critica. Questo genera una tensione produttiva più che una contraddizione».

Quale “identità culturale e pubblica” avresti voluto essere oltre a quella che ti appartiene?

«Sono attratto dall’identità del fotografo vernacolare anonimo—la persona che documentava la vita quotidiana senza pretese artistiche, creando involontariamente archivi sociali attraverso fotografie di famiglia e documentazioni amatoriali.

C’è qualcosa di affascinante nell’essere la persona dietro la macchina fotografica piuttosto che davanti, nel creare registrazioni di momenti ordinari che rivelano la loro straordinarietà solo a posteriori. Il fotografo di famiglia anonimo possedeva una sorta di libertà che a volte invidio—poteva documentare senza il peso dell’intenzione artistica o della scrutinio pubblico.

In alternativa, sono affascinato dall’identità del primo scienziato sociale o antropologo—qualcuno che poteva osservare e documentare i fenomeni sociali con la legittimità dell’indagine accademica piuttosto che dell’interpretazione artistica. In quel ruolo c’è una chiarezza che a volte appare più diretta della complessità stratificata della creazione artistica contemporanea.

Ma, in ultima analisi, queste identità alternative mi attraggono perché rappresentano modi diversi di fare ciò che già faccio: prestare attenzione a come le persone si comportano, come si relazionano con la tecnologia e come costruiscono significato attraverso le immagini. Forse ciò che desidero veramente è il permesso di essere curioso senza dover giustificare quella curiosità come arte».

Biografia

Eric Pickersgill (n. 1986, Homestead, FL) è un artista concettuale statunitense con base a Charlotte, NC. Ha conseguito un MFA presso l’Università del North Carolina a Chapel Hill (2015) e un BFA al Columbia College Chicago (2011). Il suo lavoro indaga il comportamento umano, la memoria e l’influenza della tecnologia sulla vita contemporanea attraverso fotografia, installazione e scultura.

È conosciuto soprattutto per la serie REMOVED, acclamata a livello internazionale, in cui i dispositivi digitali vengono fisicamente rimossi dalle mani dei partecipanti prima dello scatto fotografico, rivelando la disconnessione che gli schermi introducono nelle interazioni quotidiane. Le sue opere sono state presentate da CNN, BBC, The Guardian ed esposte in importanti istituzioni come il Vitra Design Museum, il V&A Dundee e il MAK (Museo Austriaco di Arti Applicate).

Tra i riconoscimenti ricevuti figurano l’ASC Regional Artist Project Grant e il NCMA Park Pictures Award. Le sue opere fanno parte di collezioni come il Museum of Fine Arts di Houston e la JPMorgan Chase Art Collection.

Due volte relatore TEDx e docente, Pickersgill è anche co-fondatore, insieme alla moglie Angie, di Pecan Print House, realtà che realizza oggetti pensati con cura per la vita contemporanea.

article_text:
Walking home after dropping his little girl at school, Peter Crome sensed he was being watched. A former professional ballet dancer now living in London, he had supplemented his income with photography work for 20 years. “But since having my daughter, my Nikon gear has sat idly by,” he says. “I got so used to lugging my heavy equipment around with me, it’s been quite refreshing to go somewhere just with a phone and still come back with wonderful pictures. My iPhone has also been a blessing for keeping in touch with family back home in Sydney,” Crome adds.

The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”

Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison. He crossed the road to draw their attention, then took a single photo on his iPhone 14 Pro. “This is the sort of picture I would have sent my mum before she passed away a couple of years ago. I think this one would have really tickled her,” Crome says.

Luca Guadagnino returns to the festival with his fascinating and of-the-moment origin story of OpenAI and its co-founder, Sam Altman.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Luca Guadagnino

Screenwriter Simon Rich

With Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Mark Rylance, Ike Barinholtz

USA-Italy 2026. 140min

Courtesy of NEON

Language English

Introduction

Artificial homes in on the rise of Open AI and the tumultuous period that saw Altman ousted as CEO of his own company. Andrew Garfield has rarely been better in his portrayal of the tech entrepreneur, with an impressive cast joining him. Writer Simon Rich and Guadagnino (Queer, LFF 2024; After the Hunt, LFF 2025) centre the human drama and ethical conundrums facing the creators of this life-changing technology.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Ce texte audacieux, dont on attend beaucoup la parution en France, débute le 12 juin 2009.Alors que la télé vit un moment historique (le passage de l’analogique au numérique), deux ados repèrent une chaîne pirate énigmatique , Public Access Afterworld. L’un d’eux disparaît peu après. Quatorze ans plus tard, Bethany, modératrice de contenu trans, découvre à son tour les ramifications de ce monde parallèle tapi derrière nos écrans.

Le livre est déjà cité parmi les dix meilleurs de l’année par Publishers Weekly. Très proche de la filmographie de Schoenbrun ( We’re All Going to the World’s Fair , I Saw the TV Glow et Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , récompensé cette année par la Queer Palm, à rattraper absolument sur MUBI ), le livre mélange science-fiction, horreur et théories du complot.

Et explorerait la dysphorie, la nostalgie des technologies rétro, l’aliénation numérique et le techno-capitalisme. Côté ciné, on rappelle que le·la cinéaste prépare « Black Hole » , une série adaptée de la BD de Charles Burns.

並行世界である3つの京都を舞台に、それぞれの世界で異なる人生を歩む女性・涼を主人公に3つのエピソードで描くドラマ。自由が確立されながらもしばしば身動きが取れなくなってしまう現代社会の片隅で小さく揺れ動く女性の生きる姿を、京都の美しい街並みの中でみずみずしく描き出す。 テーブルを挟んで向かい合う作家の桐山涼と編集者の黒川。徹夜明けの涼は、原稿への率直な意見を妙に生き生きと語る黒川に苛立ちを募らせる（episode1「窓」）。ある日突然、恋人から「今の自分では幸せにできる自信がない」とフラれてしまった涼。住み慣れた京都の街でタバコを吸いながら、幸せになるとはどういうことか、恋人が言っていた「幸せ」とは何だったのかに思いをめぐらせる（episode2「いつかの走馬灯で」）。路地裏の古びたタバコ屋で、ひとり静かに暮らす涼。朝が来たら店を開け、窓が3回鳴ったらタバコとお金を交換する。亡き母の言いつけを守り、母のように同じ日々を繰り返すことで、涼は今でも母がすぐそこに“いる”ように感じていた（episode3「エンディングはひとつだけ」）。 「魚の目」の島田愛梨珠が3編ともに主人公を演じ、「リバー、流れないでよ」の酒井善史、「キャトルミューティ玲子」の前田茉羽、Netflix映画「新幹線大爆破」の田村健太郎、「れいこいるか」の武田暁が共演。同志社女子大学出身の堀陽子が長編初監督・脚本を手がけ、主演の島田をはじめ同校の出身者や現役学生たちが制作に参加した。

article_text:
Bajo la curaduría de Brenda Fernández y por encargo del Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey (MARCO), Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte , de Wendy Cabrera Rubio, revisita la historia del Programa Bracero (1942-1964), un acuerdo entre México y Estados Unidos que permitió la contratación temporal de trabajadores mexicanos para cubrir la escasez de mano de obra durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. A partir de un episodio poco conocido de este programa —la migración de trabajadores de Nuevo León hacia Estados Unidos para trabajar en el cultivo de betabel—, la artista mexicana examina las políticas migratorias y laborales que han marcado la relación entre ambos países. Las obras conectan este capítulo histórico con el contexto sociopolítico actual, en el que persisten las tensiones en torno a la migración y los derechos de quienes sostienen la economía estadounidense con su trabajo.

A vuelo de pájaro: el norte precede la frontera

Siempre lo han sabido las aves: antes de ser frontera, el norte es una dirección en movimiento. Vuelan surcando el cielo ante líneas que, a vuelo de pájaro, resultan indistinguibles. Debajo, el territorio se extiende y continúa: desiertos, ríos, ciudades, pastizales, campos cultivados. Aquello que nos divide en gobiernos, economías, lenguas y leyes se desvanece bajo el batir de las alas.

El título de la exposición de Wendy Cabrera Rubio (Ciudad de México, 1993) en el Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey (MARCO) , curada por Brenda Fernández , Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte , nos confronta con una instancia inquietante: volar, desplazarse, parecería sencillo, incluso mundano, para aquellos cuyos cuerpos no están marcados por la jurisprudencia de la frontera ni por los límites de la ciudadanía y de una supuesta humanidad compartida. Otros cuerpos, al moverse, atraviesan alambrados documentales y físicos, inspecciones sanitarias, contratos laborales, centros de reclutamiento, exámenes médicos y categorías legales destinadas a controlar quién pasa o no al otro lado, para qué se ingresa, cuánto se permanece y qué condiciones circunscriben el regreso. Moverse, volar, ya no es dirección, sino sistema de procesamiento.

Procesar el movimiento implica, ante todo, controlar los cuerpos. Desde su exposición Mendel’s Theatre: A Twentieth-Century American Drama (2024), pasando por La señorita eugenesia y otros cuentos (2024) y Angry Young Men, Angry New Deals (2025), Cabrera Rubio ha venido examinando cómo en México y Estados Unidos los cuerpos han sido regulados científica e institucionalmente. En Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte , dicha exploración se profundiza en el caso económico, en específico en la migración laboral y en el trabajo bracero, ambos entendidos como parte de infraestructuras administrativas pertenecientes al sistema agroindustrial binacional.

A Cabrera Rubio la figura del ave le permite cuestionar ese aparente libre movimiento del trabajo migrante. En 1936, la Convention for the Protection of Migratory Birds and Game Mammals entre México y Estados Unidos convirtió incluso la circulación de las aves en materia de regulación transfronteriza; la familia Corvidae sería incluida años más tarde a través de una enmienda en 1972. Esa misma paradoja reaparece en “The Crows Fly North” (1942) de Carey McWilliams, quien propuso el vuelo estacional de las aves como metáfora de la migración de los trabajadores mexicanos que sostenían el sistema agrícola estadounidense. El norte deja entonces de ser una dirección geográfica para convertirse en un vector organizador del movimiento, el tiempo y los cuerpos de poblaciones enteras.

Esa vectorialidad adquirió otra dimensión durante la investigación de archivo que Wendy Cabrera Rubio y yo desarrollamos para este proyecto plástico. Como lugar histórico de distribución de la mano de obra en México, incluso antes de su incorporación a las redes del Programa Bracero, Monterrey ocupa un lugar central en esta historia; en la exposición, Espacio Uno del MARCO se convierte en su escenificación. La frontera se desplazaba hacia el interior del país a través de los centros de procesamiento. Como una línea de ensamblaje compuesta por salas de espera y consultorios médicos, la infraestructura migratoria organizaba cuerpos, tiempos y destinos antes incluso de que el movimiento se iniciara.

En colaboración con Yollotl Alvarado Gómez, Adrián Araiza, Pablo Arredondo Vera, Hugo Cabrera Rubio, Sbethlanna González, Nicolás Janssen, Alejandra Lomar, Candela Mirabella, Luis Alonso Sánchez y Patricia Rubio , las obras de la exposición no reconstruyen documentalmente esta historia, sino que la convierten en un escenario donde el pasado emerge como una infraestructura aún reconocible en el presente.

Melting Pot : pedagogías de control

En Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte , el carácter escénico configura uno de los núcleos expositivos. Cabrera Rubio pone en escena tanto el espectáculo del intervencionismo como las cadenas disciplinares de americanización construidas para incorporar a los trabajadores migrantes a la economía estadounidense. La videoinstalación Melting Pot y su fanzine, un folleto pedagógico coloreable para niños, condensan esta operación escénica.

En ellos, una cocina funciona como estudio televisivo y escenario de política continental: HenrYFernando Quispe, un ave bicéfala cuyo cuerpo comparten un águila calva y un cóndor andino, actúa como chef de cocina internacional dispuesto a instruirnos en la correcta alimentación. Desde la aparente sencillez del recetario, el supuesto programa educativo se descarrila en un ir y venir de contradicciones e interrupciones hasta desembocar en la violencia: el cóndor termina cocido, con su cabeza servida sobre la mesa cual San Juan Bautista.

Lo cómico se despliega precisamente en esa tensa convivencia desigual entre el águila y el cóndor, entre el dominio de Estados Unidos y la subordinación de América Latina. Entrelazados en un mismo cuerpo, la proximidad nunca elimina la asimetría, sino que vuelve visibles las condiciones de su violento funcionamiento.

Así, en Melting Pot la promesa de la receta ideal se descompone antes de servirse: abandona su pretensión de integración y aparece como una fantasía pacificada de dominio y subordinación continental. Para el trabajo bracero, esa fantasía adquiere una dimensión material. La economía estadounidense depende de la mano de obra de los trabajadores mexicanos, pero su incorporación debía administrarse estrictamente: reclutarlos, examinarlos, transportarlos y asignarlos a determinados trabajos, a la vez que se garantizaba la provisionalidad de su presencia. Aunque la fuerza laboral se incorporaba al sistema agroindustrial, para su funcionamiento ideal el trabajador debía permanecer como materia temporal y descartable.

Las obras de la exposición extienden esa lógica de administración y disciplina más allá del trabajo mismo para mostrar cómo se organizaba también la cotidianidad de los braceros: cómo debían hablar, vivir, asearse y alimentarse. La pieza de fieltro Aprenda inglés sin maestro , que remite a una fotografía de Leonard Nadel de un bracero leyendo un libro de gramática inglesa en su cama, sitúa esa pedagogía lingüística en el espacio íntimo y en el tiempo del ocio. Aprender inglés aparece como una promesa, como el aprendizaje de los códigos disciplinarios necesarios para hacerse funcional dentro de un orden laboral y social estadounidense.

Americanization and Homefront , una maleta de viaje que se convierte en maqueta a escala reitera esa misma lógica en el espacio de la vivienda mediante la arquitectura modular de las barracas militares que pone en relación los campamentos braceros con los campos de internamiento de japoneses y estadounidenses de origen japonés en Estados Unidos durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. La vivienda, y con ella el espacio de la intimidad, pasa de ser un refugio para convertirse en una tecnología de control: no solo se regula la fuerza laboral del trabajador, sino también su manera de vivir en el espacio.

La disciplina corporal se traslada a su propia representación. En colaboración con Adrián Araiza, Sbethlanna González, Alejandra Lomar y Luis Alonso Sánchez , afiches de inspiración propagandística llenan las paredes de la exhibición, construyendo un imaginario en el que el trabajador migrante debe convertirse en ícono de virtud. El trabajador rural se transforma así en sujeto de espectáculo.

El control pasa del cuerpo a la imagen misma del trabajador y de la producción agrícola. En Fruits of Eden , un photocall troquelado en fieltro remite a la espectacularización del cultivo mediante la figura del Orange Bird de Disney. La pieza dialoga también con el libro Orange Empire: California and the Fruits of Eden de Douglas Sackman, referencia fundamental para la exposición por su análisis de la construcción de California como paraíso agrícola y de sus estructuras laborales.

Reclaiming Eden , una maqueta que entrecruza referencias al Destino Manifiesto, a la conquista del oeste y a Pepe the Frog, desplaza esas idealizaciones hacia el presente, donde ciertos discursos conservadores recuperan la autosuficiencia doméstica, el retorno a la tierra y el trabajo manual como emblemas de un orden social presuntamente perdido.

La producción alimentaria rural aparece entonces como una elección individual capaz de restablecer una conexión moral con la tierra. Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte critica ese supuesto Edén que reitera una fantasía recurrente: imaginar el trabajo agrícola como una extensión natural y virtuosa de la vida, separándolo de las infraestructuras que lo organizan y de los trabajadores migrantes que lo hacen posible.

Volver a Monterrey: infraestructuras de frontera

En el terreno del espectáculo diplomático, dicha relación entre infraestructura y representación reaparece en La histórica visita de Roosevelt a Monterrey . Frente a la imagen pública del encuentro entre los presidentes Franklin D. Roosevelt y Manuel Ávila Camacho, la cooperación binacional se muestra como puesta en escena, mientras que los contratos, los centros de reclutamiento, los exámenes médicos y los circuitos administrativos que hicieron posible la circulación de trabajadores permanecen fuera de la tarima.

Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte expone cómo el trabajador y su fuerza de trabajo aparecen constantemente de manera tangencial: en formularios, recetas médicas, programas de gobierno y fotografías presidenciales. Sus cuerpos no desaparecen; las fotografías de Leonard Nadel han hecho proliferar su imagen. Pero esa visibilidad conlleva una extraña desaparición: el trabajador se subordina a los dispositivos que lo observan, lo clasifican y organizan su circulación.

Dos títeres de cuervo sobrevuelan la exposición junto con HenrYFernando Quispe, atravesando un mismo territorio: el águila y el cóndor vigilan a aquellos cuervos en su vuelo hacia el norte. Los inscriben en una integración continental. El vuelo se transforma así en una herramienta de vigilancia. Estas aves ahora se ciernen sobre Monterrey recordándonos que, como muestra la obra Deuda histórica , el trabajo migrante continúa siendo marginado en las historias de ambos países.

A vuelo de pájaro, la frontera ya no parece invisible. Retomando el movimiento anunciado por su título, en Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte las aves siguen una dirección, pero su vuelo revela que, para algunos cuerpos, la frontera los precede: se extiende a través de los dispositivos que anticipan, administran y condicionan cada uno de sus movimientos.

Los cuervos vuelan hacia el norte , de Wendy Cabrera Rubio, se presentó del 22 de mayo al 20 de septiembre de 2026 en el Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey ( MARCO ).

article_text:
At the Eubie Blake Cultural Center in Baltimore, Maryland, ‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ brought ten artists from Baltimore and Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley into dialogue about identity, memory, and creative freedom.

What emerges when ten distinct artistic voices share a space? Through painting, photography, abstraction, and mixed media, ‘5 × 5 Baltimore’ explored the breadth of Black male experience, tracing personal histories, cultural inheritance, and expressions of joy, vulnerability, and transformation. In conversation with ART AFRICA , co-curators Barbara Bullard and Derek Price discuss the relationships behind the exhibition and the importance of allowing artists to shape the terms of their own representation. Exhibition view of ‘ 5 x 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men ‘, 2026. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

Brendon Bell-Roberts: What brought the ten artists in ‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ together, and how did the exhibition form around their practices?

‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ evolved from the 4 × 5 Exhibition, originally presented at Eleven20 Studios and Gallery in Easton, Pennsylvania, in May 2025. Curated by Danny Moyer and co-curated by artist Al Johnson, the exhibition brought together five accomplished artists of the African Diaspora rooted in the Lehigh Valley.

After experiencing the original exhibition and through conversations with artist Al Johnson and Barbara Bullard, Alma Roberts, our Exhibition Advisor, recognized an opportunity to expand its concept by bringing the work of Lehigh Valley artists into dialogue with five artists from Baltimore’s Black artistic community. Alma subsequently approached Derek Price, Executive Director of the Eubie Blake Cultural Center, about presenting an expanded exhibition at the Center. That conversation became the foundation for ‘5 × 5 Baltimore’.

Working with Alma, we approached the selection of artists collaboratively, seeking distinctive artistic voices whose practices could contribute to a meaningful exchange. Each artist then selected the works that would represent his individual practice. This was important to us. We wanted the exhibition to reflect not only our shared curatorial vision but also the artists’ own understanding of their creative identities.

The resulting exhibition brought together Lehigh Valley mixed media artist Al Johnson, multidisciplinary artist Anthony Smith Jr., fine arts photographer Charles Stonewall, abstract artist Femi J. Johnson, and surrealist artist Rigo Peralta, and five artists who proudly call Baltimore home: multidisciplinary artist Ainsley Burrows, painter/muralist Ernest Shaw, multidisciplinary artist Jeffrey Kent, painter Jerry Prettyman, and mixed media artist Larry “Poncho” Brown. This extraordinary convergence of artistic perspectives created a vibrant exchange of techniques, ideas, and emotions.

Their works span themes of loss, healing, joy, and transformation, each reflecting personal and collective journeys. Rather than presenting Black male identity as a monolithic experience, we sought to create a dialogue across geography, generations, and artistic disciplines that preserved each artist’s individuality while revealing unexpected connections among their practices.

What emerged was more than a gathering of accomplished artists. The exhibition offered an opportunity to challenge, celebrate, and elevate the lived experiences of Black men in America while expanding the conversation about identity, representation, and creative freedom. Exhibition view of ‘ 5 x 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men ‘, 2026. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

Baltimore and the Lehigh Valley have distinct cultural histories as well as shared histories of migration, labour and struggle. In what ways did these connections shape the exhibition’s curatorial framework?

Although geographically distinct, Baltimore and Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley share intertwined histories shaped by industry, migration, resilience, and cultural self-determination. Both regions have cultivated vibrant Black artistic communities, grounded in traditions of community-driven arts practice and the determination to create spaces for cultural expression.

These shared histories provided an important foundation for our curatorial approach. Rather than emphasizing geographical distinctions, we sought to create an environment in which the artists’ individual practices could enter into meaningful dialogue. We deliberately intermingled the works of Baltimore and Lehigh Valley artists throughout the gallery, allowing relationships to emerge through artistic expression, subject matter, and visual language rather than regional affiliation.

The relationship between place, community, and artistic expression is reflected in works such as Ernest Shaw’s Crossing Godz 6 , which portrays two Baltimore squeegee workers, bringing a distinctly local experience into the gallery while inviting broader reflection on visibility and representation. Anthony Smith Jr.’s August Mexico City , a layered paper quilt inspired by memories of travel, friendships, and encounters with place, approaches community through personal connections and experiences that extend beyond geographical boundaries. Though different in subject and artistic language, both works demonstrate how individual experiences of place can shape creative expression.

‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ honours creative sovereignty and celebrates the ways artists of the African Diaspora build community, mentor youth, and forge space where none was offered. Baltimore’s vibrant Black artistic ecosystem provided a meaningful setting for this exchange, while the participating artists brought perspectives extending beyond regional boundaries to engage broader themes of identity, belonging, resilience, and transformation.

Ultimately, our curatorial framework reflected the belief that these two artistic communities had much to contribute to one another. Our intention was not to erase the distinctions between these communities, but to create a space where their shared histories and individual artistic voices could inform, challenge, and enrich one another. Anthony Smith Jr, ‘ August Mexico City ‘, 2024 – 2026. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

How did you connect painting, mixed media, abstraction, photography and figurative practice in the gallery?

Our approach to installing ‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ was both intentional and intuitive. We wanted the gallery to become a space where painting, mixed media, abstraction, photography, and figurative practices could engage one another without being confined by medium, geography, or artistic style.

The process was deeply collaborative, organic, and improvisational. Barbara would often sit on the gallery floor, absorbing the energy of the space and considering how the works might speak to one another. Derek approached the installation with a similarly intuitive sensibility. As the exhibition took shape, we moved artworks throughout the gallery, experimenting with arrangements and discovering unexpected relationships. Much like musicians responding to one another, we brought distinct perspectives to the process, yet our instincts were remarkably aligned, and most decisions were made in unison.

Rather than separating works by discipline or region, we intermingled the artists’ practices, allowing contrasts in materials, imagery, scale, and expression to create a visual dialogue. Jeffrey Kent’s Black Joy , incorporating glitter, shredded currency, and text, exemplifies the expressive possibilities of mixed media, while Femi J. Johnson’s Ruff Neck Delight represents a distinctly abstract approach. These different visual languages illustrate the range of artistic practices we sought to bring into conversation. We were interested in how an abstract work might influence the experience of a figurative piece, or how photography and mixed media could offer different perspectives on identity, memory, and representation. Each work was considered both individually and in relation to those surrounding it.

There was something especially meaningful about undertaking this process within a cultural institution honouring Eubie Blake, an iconic Black musician and composer whose artistry persevered through the constraints of Jim Crow. His legacy provided a powerful historical context for an exhibition celebrating the individuality, creative freedom, and artistic achievements of contemporary Black men.

The resulting installation reflected the essence of our co-curatorial partnership: two distinct perspectives working in concert to create a cohesive experience while allowing each artist’s voice to remain unmistakably his own. Femi J Johnson, ‘ Ruff Neck Delight ‘, 2021. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

Black male identity is often discussed through broad social or political categories. How does ‘5 × 5 Baltimore’ address individual experience?

‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ approaches Black male identity through the specificity of lived experience rather than through inherited social or political frameworks. While the participating artists may share certain cultural and historical experiences, we recognise that their individual perspectives, personal histories, and artistic expressions cannot be defined by a singular narrative.

Central to our curatorial approach was the commitment to allowing the artists to speak for themselves. Alongside their artwork, the exhibition featured video interviews that offered visitors an opportunity to hear directly from the artists, providing insight into the personal experiences and creative journeys that inform their practices. These recorded reflections complemented the artworks, foregrounding the interior narratives that shape each artist’s trajectory.

The works collectively trace a spectrum of emotional and psychological experiences, including loss, healing, joy, resilience, and transformation. Ainsley Burrows’s Shadow Work , for example, explores introspection and transformation through a fractured figurative composition. Rigo Peralta’s La Flor Dominica #2 draws on a distinctly different visual language, reflecting his broader engagement with Afro-Caribbean cultural heritage and symbolism. Although their approaches differ, both demonstrate how individual artistic expression can complicate and expand our understanding of Black identity. Importantly, the exhibition also affirms that a Black male artist’s creative practice need not be confined to representations of Black men. His artistic identity encompasses the full range of subjects, experiences, and ideas he chooses to explore.

As co-curators, we wanted to create a space where shared cultural experiences could coexist with individual expression, without diminishing either. The exhibition positions these men not as representatives of a category, but as creators whose personal histories generate the conceptual and aesthetic frameworks of their work. Rigo Peralta , ‘ La Flor Dominica #2′ , 2025. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

How do cultural identity, belonging and tenacity emerge across the artists’ practices and perspectives?

‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ reveals cultural identity, belonging, and tenacity not as abstract themes but as lived conditions that shape each artist’s practice. Across the exhibition, these ideas emerge through personal narratives—how memory, place, and community imprint themselves on artistic expression.

Cultural identity is reflected in the artists’ distinct visual languages and connections to heritage and community. Jerry Prettyman’s Eternal Wisdom explores the transmission of ancestral knowledge through women and oral traditions, emphasising the importance of preserving cultural memory across generations. Al Johnson’s mixed-media works incorporate sheet music handwritten by his father, connecting family memory with artistic inheritance.

Belonging emerges through relationships and responsibilities within communities. Larry “Poncho” Brown’s Saving Our Sons , depicting a central figure embracing four younger men, speaks to protection and intergenerational care. Tenacity finds a quieter expression in Charles Stonewall’s Surviving Times of Deepest Despair , inviting reflection on isolation, perseverance, and hope.

What connects these varied practices is the artists’ ability to transform personal experience into expressions that resonate beyond the individual. Their works reveal belonging not simply as a connection to a particular place, but as something sustained through family, cultural inheritance, shared responsibility, and the determination to preserve one’s identity.

Together, these artistic perspectives demonstrate that cultural identity, belonging, and tenacity are neither fixed nor universally experienced. They are continually shaped and redefined through the lives, relationships, and creative choices of the artists themselves. Larry ‘Poncho’ Brown, ‘ Saving Our Sons ‘, 2005. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

What emerged from placing together works that engage stereotype, transformation, memory and representation?

Placed in dialogue, the works reveal how stereotype, transformation, memory, and representation operate as interconnected forces rather than isolated themes. What emerged was a collective reorientation: distinct artistic voices challenging inherited narratives, reclaiming personal and communal histories, and asserting the specificity of individual experience.

Anthony Smith Jr.’s Mammy Poisons With Love And The Schwartz employs satire and exaggerated imagery to expose the absurdity of racial stereotypes. In contrast, Larry “Poncho” Brown’s Always Reading Between the Lines constructs a powerful Black male figure from fragments of printed media, his upward gaze suggesting defiance and self-determination. These works approach representation differently, yet both invite viewers to reconsider how Black men are seen and understood.

As co-curators, we were particularly struck by how these varied expressions could coexist without diminishing one another. Some works confront difficult histories directly; others invite contemplation, celebrate cultural inheritance, or explore the possibilities of transformation. Their proximity created a dialogue that was sometimes challenging, sometimes affirming, but always rooted in the individuality of the artists.

Together, the works generated a shared insistence on complexity, showing Black men shaping, revising, and expanding the terms of their own representation. What gave the exhibition its power was not a single message, but the opportunity to encounter these different perspectives within a shared cultural space. Anthony Smith Jr, ‘ Mammy Poisons With Love And The Schwartz Mixed ‘, 2023. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

You have described the exhibition as “locally grounded and globally resonant.” How do you understand the relationship between these communities and wider conversations around Black identity and cultural expression?

When we describe ‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’ as “locally grounded and globally resonant,” we’re speaking to the way these artists’ practices emerge from very specific communities while also engaging conversations that extend far beyond any single city. Baltimore and the Lehigh Valley share intertwined histories shaped by migration, labour, and cultural self-determination, and those histories have produced rich ecosystems of Black artistic practice. The participating artists draw from these environments—communities where they build networks of care, mentor youth, and create space where none was offered.

At the same time, the work is globally resonant because the questions these artists navigate, including visibility, inheritance, resilience, and self-determination, extend across the African Diaspora. Black men in different countries encounter distinct histories, cultural expectations, and challenges to their identity and representation. Their experiences are not identical, yet their artistic practices can contribute to broader conversations about how Black men define themselves within and against structures that attempt to limit their complexity.

These connections emerge through the works themselves. Jerry Prettyman’s Maiden Voyage confronts the history of the transatlantic slave trade and its enduring consequences across the African Diaspora. Ainsley Burrows’s The Long and Complicated History of America explores the turbulence and unresolved contradictions of American history, inviting reflection on how national histories continue to shape Black identity and experience. Femi J. Johnson’s abstract practice, informed by ancestral connections, music, and improvisation, offers another perspective on cultural inheritance and the ways artistic expression can transcend geographical boundaries.

Through the collective presentation of these ten artists, the exhibition shows how local communities contribute to, and expand, the wider discourse on Black identity. Their distinct practices demonstrate that global resonance does not require a singular Black male experience. Rather, it emerges through the recognition of shared concerns alongside meaningful differences in history, culture, and individual expression.

For us, the global is not an abstraction; it is built from the accumulation of specific, place-based experiences that, when seen collectively, illuminate the vast and interconnected landscape of Black creative sovereignty. Ainsley Burrows, ‘ The Long and Complicated History of America ‘, 2026. Image courtesy of Eubie Blake Cultural Center.

Dialogue is central to the exhibition and its accompanying public programme. What conversations do you hope ‘5 × 5 Baltimore’ will continue to spark among the artists, audiences and communities involved?

Dialogue is central to ‘5 × 5 Baltimore: The Art of Black Men’, both within the exhibition and across its public programming. We hope it continues to spark meaningful conversations among artists, audiences, and communities that extend well beyond the exhibition itself.

Among the artists, we want to sustain the cross-regional exchange between Baltimore and the Lehigh Valley. One of the most rewarding aspects of the exhibition was witnessing the genuine camaraderie and mutual respect among the participating artists. Their conversations about one another’s work and creative approaches demonstrated how artistic exchange can foster meaningful relationships and new possibilities for collaboration.

For audiences, we hope the work encourages a more nuanced understanding of Black male identity, prompting conversations about visibility, inheritance, resilience, and self-determination that extend into classrooms, community spaces, and everyday life. We want visitors to consider how personal histories shape artistic expression, how stereotypes can obscure individuality, and how these artists use their work to reclaim narratives, express vulnerability, celebrate joy, and affirm their own identities.

Within communities, our hope is that ‘5 × 5 Baltimore ’ inspires continued dialogue about how communities can support artists, how artists can support one another, and how cultural institutions can meaningfully invest in Black creative sovereignty. These conversations should extend to practical commitments, including mentorship, sustained exhibition opportunities, connections with collectors, and greater investment in the cultural spaces that nurture Black artistic expression.

We also envision ‘5 × 5 Baltimore’ as an evolving exhibition model. As the concept expands across the Mid-Atlantic and beyond, we hope to welcome five additional local artists in each new city, extending the platform to accomplished Black male artists whose perspectives enrich the cultural dialogue. Each iteration could become a site of exchange, where regionally rooted and nationally recognised artists intersect to challenge, celebrate, and elevate the lived experiences of Black men.

Looking further ahead, we hope to extend this dialogue internationally, exploring both the common themes and distinct experiences that shape Black male identity across different countries and cultures. Future iterations could introduce broader themes, interdisciplinary partnerships, and immersive programming designed to connect communities through the power of art.

We want these conversations to contribute to a shared language of cultural expression, rooted in local histories yet in dialogue with global movements in Black art, thought, and representation. That is the enduring work of ‘5 × 5 Baltimore ’ : to keep these conversations alive, expansive, and generative.

This exhibition was on view at the Eubie Blake Cultural Center in Baltimore, Maryland, from 20th June until 22nd August 2026.
